clue.text: Tilt rear lens again to view beyond the solar system

indicators.note: 'again' asks for the same letters a second time over, and the only thing that can be fresh about them is the order they come in.

parts.note: twelve letters of fodder

explanation.surface: An astronomer angling the back element of a telescope for another look at the far sky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tilt' is the word that looks like the instruction, and it is fodder; the small word 'again' is what does the shuffling. Twelve-letter anagrams rarely announce themselves this quietly.
explanation.definitionFit: Interstellar means lying between the stars, which is everything outside the sun's own family of planets.

clue.text: Goat's rib extends inwards

indicators.note: 'inwards' points away from the surface of the words to what lies within them, so the letters are sitting inside rather than waiting to be assembled.

parts.note: four consecutive letters, starting inside the first word and finishing inside the second

explanation.surface: An anatomy note about the way a goat's ribcage curves.
explanation.walkthrough: Hidden answers like to straddle a word break, because the eye reads whole words and skips over the join. The ibex is the wild goat of the Alps and the Middle East, famous for its long ridged horns.
explanation.definitionFit: An ibex is a wild mountain goat, so the bare word names the animal exactly rather than by example.

clue.text: Treatment getting the blame at end of day

parts.note: the definite article, taken over as it stands
to take the rap is to take the blame for something

indicators.note: 'end of' names the finish of the word that follows, so one letter is taken from the back of it.

parts.note: the last letter of 'day'

explanation.surface: Someone left carrying the can for a mistake as the working day closes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The blame' reads as one phrase, which is what hides the fact that the article is a separate piece. RAP for blame comes from the American courtroom slang that gave us rap sheet and bum rap.
explanation.definitionFit: Therapy is the course of treatment a patient is put through, whether by talking, drugs or exercise.

clue.text: My! Her awful verse!

indicators.note: something awful is badly made, and letters called awful have been put together wrongly — in an order other than their own.

parts.note: five letters of fodder, the exclamation mark sitting across the join

explanation.surface: A reader recoiling at a woman's dreadful poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My!' and 'Her' read as two separate outbursts, and that punctuation is exactly what stops them being seen as one five-letter heap. The exclamation marks carry no instruction at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhyme is a short piece of verse, the word standing for the whole poem as well as for the chime at its line ends.

clue.text: Fashionable attempt to hide tail

indicators.note: to hide a thing is to put it out of sight inside something else, so one word closes over the other.

parts.note: an attempt at something is a try at it
the tail of anything is its end

explanation.surface: A creature making a smart job of tucking its tail out of sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tail' is not asking for a last letter here, which is its usual crossword job — it is a whole three-letter word. The split falls after the first two letters of the outer word, which is why nothing looks like a seam.
explanation.definitionFit: Trendy is the informal word for whatever is in fashion at the moment, so it takes the place of 'fashionable' exactly.

clue.text: Once-over to observe twice

indicators.note: 'twice' says the word in front of it is to be obeyed a second time, so two different synonyms for it sit end to end.

parts.note: to observe something is to look at it
the second time round the same word is read again, and to observe is also to see

explanation.surface: An instruction to give something a second inspection.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves mean the same thing, which is what lets the clue name the instruction once and count it twice. The 4-3 enumeration is the only warning that two words are coming.
explanation.definitionFit: A once-over is a quick inspection, and the answer is the same casual glance under a jokier name.

clue.text: In Vietnam, I got to see Spanish friend

indicators.note: 'In' reads as a place in the surface, but its job is to say the letters are already sitting inside the words that follow.

parts.note: five consecutive letters, running out of the end of the country's name and through the two short words after it

explanation.surface: A traveller recalling the people met on a trip to Vietnam.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma is there to stop the eye running the words together, which is the only defence a hidden answer has. Spanish in a Vietnamese setting is the mismatch that makes the definition hard to spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Amigo is simply the Spanish for friend, borrowed into English as a matey form of address.

clue.text: Backs down about loaned shilling

parts.note: re = about, the word at the head of a memo
money loaned has been lent
s = shilling, the abbreviation printed on British prices before decimalisation

explanation.surface: Someone giving way in a squabble over a borrowed coin.
explanation.walkthrough: A shilling was the British coin worth twelve old pence, killed off in 1971 and kept alive in crosswords as its single letter. Three pieces in a row, none of them longer than four letters, is the hardest shape to spot.
explanation.definitionFit: To relent is to give way after holding out, which is what backing down in an argument amounts to.

clue.text: Song of lamentation, say, in cathedral

indicators.note: 'in' puts what comes before it inside what comes after, so one piece is buried in the middle of the other.

parts.note: Ely is the cathedral city in the Cambridgeshire fens, its three letters a crossword staple
eg = say, both meaning 'for example'

explanation.surface: A mourning song being sung inside a cathedral.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' is a instruction, not part of the picture: it is the Latin abbreviation for 'for example'. The cathedral's own name splits neatly in two around it, which is why the seam is invisible.
explanation.definitionFit: An elegy is a poem or song written in mourning for someone who has died, so lamentation is its entire purpose.

clue.text: Controversial English reason

parts.note: e = English, the usual single letter for the language or the nation
the reason someone does a thing is their motive for it

explanation.surface: An English justification for something, of the kind that starts arguments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reason' here is the thing that drives an action rather than the faculty of thinking, which is what lets it stand in for a motive. A three-word clue with no indicator at all is a charade every time.
explanation.definitionFit: An emotive subject is one that raises strong feeling on both sides, and that is what makes it controversial — the match is by consequence rather than by dictionary.

clue.text: Cabbage I scooped out from visual toy

parts.note: kale is the curly-leaved cabbage, and the crossword's cabbage of choice at four letters

indicators.note: 'out' here means out of true, out of order — letters marked out will not stay as they were handed over.

parts.note: the pronoun hands over its own single letter
seven letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A cook describing the cabbage they hollowed out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scooped out' reads as one kitchen action, and the two words are doing quite separate jobs. A lone 'I' in a clue is almost always a letter rather than a narrator.
explanation.definitionFit: A kaleidoscope is the tube of mirrors and coloured chips you turn to watch the pattern change, sold for a century as a child's toy.

clue.text: Keep watching this lizard

definitions.meaning: to keep something under continuous observation — a patient, a situation, a bank account
the large tropical reptiles of the genus Varanus, the Komodo dragon among them

explanation.surface: Someone told to keep their eyes on a lizard.
explanation.walkthrough: The monitor lizard is said to have got its name from an old belief that it warns of crocodiles nearby, so the two senses share an ancestor rather than merely colliding. Double definitions with that link are rare.
explanation.definitionFit: To monitor is to keep something under continuous watch, and a monitor is also the big tropical lizard that the word names as a noun.

clue.text: Information found behind animal, yak initially, for gas

indicators.note: what is found behind something has been reached after it, so the piece named first is placed last in the answer.

parts.note: an ox is an animal, and the two-letter beast of burden is the setter's usual choice

indicators.note: 'initially' means at the outset, so only the opening letter of the word in front of it is taken.

parts.note: the opening letter of 'yak'
gen is British informal for information — give me the gen on it

explanation.surface: Notes jotted down behind an animal, a yak to begin with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Behind' is the instruction that sends the information to the back of the answer, not filler holding the sentence together. Two animals are named and only one of them is wanted whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxygen is the gas that makes up a fifth of the air, so the bare word 'gas' defines it by the family it belongs to.

clue.text: Angered, possibly yes!

indicators.note: possibly says the word angered is one possible arrangement of the letters, so they are reordered

parts.note: taken as written: its seven letters are the fodder

explanation.surface: Someone asked whether they were angered answers 'possibly — yes!'.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue works twice: rearranging the letters of 'Angered' gives a word that itself means angered, and the closing 'yes!' confirms that the anagram is also the meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Enraged is a direct synonym of angered, meaning made furious.

clue.text: In France I make a mess of test for high flyers

definitions.note: The jet set is a collective singular, so the plural definition names the people in the group rather than matching the phrase's own grammar.

parts.note: je is the French for I, and 'in France' is the standard way of asking for the French word

indicators.note: to make a mess of something is to leave it disordered, and letters left disordered come out in a new arrangement.

parts.note: four letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A French student making a hash of an exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In France I' is a formula worth learning: it never means a holiday, only the French word for whatever follows. 'High flyers' is doing two jobs, the literal aircraft and the figurative standing.
explanation.definitionFit: The jet set are the wealthy who fly off to fashionable places, so 'high flyers' names them by the aeroplanes and by their social altitude at once.

clue.text: Sign of venomous creature losing tail

indicators.note: 'losing' means the thing named next is gone, struck off the word that came before it.

parts.note: the desert arachnid with the sting in its curled-up tail
the tail of a word is its final letter, and here that is the N at the end of the creature

explanation.surface: A venomous creature that has somehow lost its tail.
explanation.walkthrough: The sting really is in a scorpion's tail, so the picture and the instruction are the same image — a rare case where the surface helps rather than hinders. 'Sign' on its own is enough to mean the zodiac.
explanation.definitionFit: Scorpio is one of the twelve signs of the zodiac, the one covering birthdays from late October to late November.

clue.text: Lisbon sailor circling tiny tree

indicators.note: what circles a thing has closed all the way round it, so the answer sits enclosed by the words on either side of it.

parts.note: six consecutive letters, beginning inside the city's name and ending inside the sailor

explanation.surface: A sailor from Lisbon walking round a miniature tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circling' is not asking for a reversal or a container — it says the answer is enclosed by what surrounds it. A Portuguese city and a sailor are a plausible enough pair to read straight past.
explanation.definitionFit: A bonsai is a tree kept deliberately dwarf in a shallow pot, which is exactly what the Japanese word names.

clue.text: Entertainer not being himself makes terrapins moo!

indicators.note: something not being itself is not in its own proper shape, and letters out of their own shape have been put in a different order.

parts.note: twelve letters of fodder

explanation.surface: An entertainer drops the act and a tankful of terrapins starts lowing like cattle.
explanation.walkthrough: The indicator is also a description of the trade: a man not being himself is both the picture and the instruction to the letters. Terrapins are the small freshwater turtles, and a mooing one is the setter's decoy.
explanation.definitionFit: An impersonator makes a living doing other people's voices and faces on stage, so 'entertainer' names the trade directly.

clue.text: Boy entering river softly

indicators.note: what enters a thing has gone inside it, so the piece named before it is placed within the piece named after.

parts.note: the Po is Italy's longest river and the crossword's shortest
Ian, one of the stock crossword boys alongside Al, Len and Des

explanation.surface: A lad wading quietly into a river.
explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces are Italian: the Po runs across the north of the country, and piano is the direction written in a score. The instrument took its name from being able to play both piano and forte, soft and loud.
explanation.definitionFit: Piano is the marking that tells a player to perform softly, an adverb English took straight from Italian and never translated.

clue.text: An area of the North Sea covered with water

parts.note: the indefinite article, spelt with the extra letter here only because 'area' begins with a vowel
the Wash is the square bay biting into England's east coast between Norfolk and Lincolnshire

explanation.surface: A stretch of the North Sea, and the unremarkable news that there is water on it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface says nothing at all — of course an area of sea is covered with water — and that blandness is what keeps the bay out of sight. Setters reach for the Wash whenever four letters of British coast are needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Something awash is flooded: water is standing over it rather than merely wetting it.

clue.text: Can room be purchased on the radio?

indicators.note: a thing on the radio is heard and never seen, so the word is wanted for its sound rather than its spelling.

parts.note: goods that can be purchased are goods you sell, and SELL said aloud is spelt this other way

explanation.surface: Someone asking whether accommodation is up for sale over the airwaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the radio' is the sound signal here, not a hint about broadcasting: what you hear is a verb and what you write is a noun. Monks and prisoners both live in one.
explanation.definitionFit: A cell is the small bare room a monk or a prisoner lives in, so 'room' is the plain sense with all the trimmings taken off.

clue.text: Love varieties of fruit

parts.note: love is nothing in tennis, written as the round nought
the ranges of something are the varieties it comes in

explanation.surface: A declaration of fondness for several different kinds of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Varieties of fruit' reads as a single phrase and is two separate jobs, one of them the definition. Love for nought comes from tennis, where the score is said to be the shape of an egg.
explanation.definitionFit: Oranges are a fruit, so the definition names the family the answer belongs to rather than pinning down the kind.

clue.text: Politician gets in drink, more than enough

indicators.note: to get in is to find a way inside, so the piece named before it ends up surrounded by the piece named after.

parts.note: ale is the setter's default three-letter drink
MP = Member of Parliament, the British politician's two letters

explanation.surface: An MP squeezing into a crowded bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets in' is doing double duty on the surface: it is what a candidate does at an election as well as what the letters do here. The drink splits after its first letter, which is where the join hides.
explanation.definitionFit: Ample means there is more of a thing than the occasion actually calls for — enough, and then some over.

clue.text: Pet's home that lacks privacy?

definitions.meaning: read straight, the round glass tank that sits on a windowsill
the sense the setter is after: the phrase is used of any life lived where everybody can see in, from a royal marriage to an open-plan office

explanation.surface: A pet kept somewhere with nothing at all to hide behind.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase works twice over: it is the literal container and the standing metaphor for a life in full view. With no wordplay to take apart, the 8,4 enumeration is the only mechanical help on offer.
explanation.definitionFit: A goldfish bowl is both the pet's glass home and the everyday metaphor for an existence with no privacy in it.
